questions.question: 3. Vaccines

parts.text: a) What is thimerosal?
b) What vaccines contain thimerosal?

cohort_answer.text:
Thimerosal is an ethyl mercury derivative (organic-mercury compound), a preservative used only in multi-dose vials of vaccines. Low doses have not been shown to produce negative health effects. Ethylmercury cleared from body more quickly than methylmercury. Prevents bacterial growth in vaccines. Taken out of vaccines in children by 2001
Some multidose preparations of influenza or hepatitis B vaccines are the only thimerosal-containing products that might be offered to children as part of routine schedule. No vaccine in Canada since March 2001 for routine use in children contains thimerosal, except some influenza vaccines. DTaP, polio, Hib have not contained it since 1997-98. MMR, inactivated polio, pneumococcal vaccines used in Canada never contained thimerosal

parts.text: Define conjugated vaccines

cohort_answer.text: A) Conjugated vaccines are polysaccharides combined with an immunologically active protein carrier to improve vaccine effectiveness - combining a weak antigen (polysaccharide) with a strong antigen (protein carrier) for a stronger immune response. questions.question: Live vs inactivated and protein vs polysaccharide vaccines

parts.text: Why is live vaccine better than inactivated?
Why is protein better than polysaccharide vaccine?
Most likely complication from MMRV?

cohort_answer.text: A) Live vaccines are more similar to the disease-causing pathogen, creating a stronger and longer-lasting immune response. B) Protein (conjugate) vaccines have an added protein antigen attached to a weaker polysaccharide antigen, eliciting a stronger response than polysaccharide alone; protein antigens generate T-lymphocyte-dependent immune response with immunologic memory, booster effects, and good immunogenicity across ages; polysaccharide vaccines induce T-lymphocyte-independent response without immune memory or boosting, and have poor immunogenicity in infants/young children. C) Febrile seizures (also fever, arthralgias, LAD, rash; rare: hypersensitivity reactions, ITP).

cohort_answer.text: A) Dukoral is a killed whole-cell oral vaccine with the nontoxic B subunit of cholera toxin, providing limited (<50%) protection against ETEC. CtxA cleaved into subunits activates G-protein coupled adenylyl cyclase increasing cAMP, activating chloride/water secretion via CFTR; CTxB binds GM1 receptors; antibodies against CTxB provide cross protection for ETEC toxin. B) Vaccine efficacy against all-cause diarrhea ~6%; protection against O1 Vibrio cholerae 64-85%; protection against ETEC ~25%; limited value, consider for selected high-risk short-term travellers >2 years (chronic illness, increased acquisition risk, immunosuppressed, hx repeated severe TD, brief illness intolerable). C) ETEC accounts for 25-50% of traveler's diarrhea (depends on destination).

questions.question: Thumbnail of measles

parts.text: Name 4 classic symptoms
Name 4 potential severe complications
Name a test other than serology and give two potential sample sites for this test
What is post-exposure prophylaxis (48h post) for an unvaccinated 2-year-old girl?
What is post-exposure prophylaxis (5 days post) for a healthy, non-pregnant woman who works in daycare?

cohort_answer.text:
Four classic symptoms: Conjunctivitis; Cough; Coryza; Maculopapular rash that begins on the face and spreads; Koplik spots; Fever
Four severe complications: Pneumonia; Acute encephalitis; Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (late complication); Myocarditis; Otitis media; Laryngotracheobronchitis; Diarrhoea
Test other than serology: RT-PCR. Sites: heparinized blood, nasopharyngeal aspirates, throat swabs, and urine
Post-exposure prophylaxis 48h (unvaccinated 2yo girl): MMR vaccine (ideally within 72 hours of exposure). Notes: Except in healthcare settings, unvaccinated people who receive their first dose of MMR vaccine within 72 hours after exposure may return to childcare, school, or work. Immunoglobulin (within 6 days of exposure): People who are at risk for severe illness and complications from measles, such as infants younger than 12 months of age, pregnant women without evidence of measles immunity, and people with severely compromised immune systems, should receive immunoglobulin. (MMR vaccine can be given instead if between 6 months and 12 months age). After receipt of IG, people cannot return to healthcare settings. In other settings, eg childcare, school, or work, factors such as immune status, intense or prolonged contact, and presence of populations at risk, should be taken into consideration before allowing people to return. Exclude healthcare personnel without evidence of immunity from duty from day 5 after first exposure to day 21 after last exposure, regardless of post-exposure vaccine.
Post-exposure prophylaxis 5 days (healthy non-pregnant woman working in daycare): If immunocompetent, susceptible – vaccinate to protect (PHAC recommendations is to vaccinate up to 6 days, but will also protect from future episodes). IVIG is for severely immunocompromised / pregnant woman or <6mos

parts.text: What is the main difference in formulation between the varicella vaccine and the live shingles vaccine?
What vaccine to give in: 30F with varicella IgG negative, not pregnant
What vaccine to give in: 51M with previous chickenpox

questions.model_answer:
a) The recombinant/live shingles vaccine formulations differ in that the live attenuated zoster vaccine (Zostavax) contains a much higher titre (~14-fold) of the same Oka varicella-zoster strain than the varicella vaccine (Varivax), needed to boost the already-primed but waning cell-mediated immunity in older adults; the newer recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) instead uses a non-live VZV glycoprotein E antigen with an adjuvant.

c) 51M with prior chickenpox: no varicella vaccine needed (immune from natural infection); not yet in the standard age range for routine zoster vaccination (typically recommended starting age 50 for Shingrix), so no zoster vaccine indicated purely based on this history.
d) 68F, varicella IgG negative, not immunocompromised: give the 2-dose varicella (Varivax) vaccine series, as she is non-immune and has no contraindication to a live vaccine.
e) Advantages of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) over live attenuated (Zostavax): (1) Significantly higher efficacy against herpes zoster (>90% vs ~50%). (2) Can be safely given to immunocompromised individuals (non-live vaccine). (3) More durable, longer-lasting protection over time.

parts.text: Should you give conjugate, polysaccharide, or both? Explain

questions.model_answer: Give both. Rationale: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13/PCV20) induces T-cell dependent immune memory and a more robust, longer-lasting response, and should be given first; pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) broadens serotype coverage (23 serotypes vs 13-20 in conjugate) but produces a T-cell independent, less durable response without immune memory. parts.text: A. Two possible explanations for this

cohort_answer.text:
A: Waning immunity. Vaccine non-responder (< 10% with standard 3 dose series)

B: Repeat HBsAb, HBsAg, HBcAb and obtain liver enzymes. If all negative (i.e. anti-HBs < 10), would complete second series of 3 vaccines and test for seroconversion 1-2 months after completion of series. There is some evidence that non-responders exhibit a better response when HBV/HAV vaccine given e.g. Twinrix. JID 2008 PMID 18544037. Non-responders include advanced age, smoking/higher BMI, chronic disease like CKD and other immunosuppression, celiac disease, genetic HLA variants
